newsitem.title: Italy: Italian PM raises Yugoslavia in attack on Bossi.
newsitem.headline: Italian PM raises Yugoslavia in attack on Bossi.

text.p: A warning from Prime Minister Romano Prodi that Italy must not go the way of Yugoslavia raised the political heat on Thursday before a planned "declaration of independence" by northern secessionists on Sunday.

Prodi's reference to the wars that devastated Italy's neighbour injected an element of unease into the government's attitude to Northern League leader Umberto Bossi's drive for a separate "republic of Padania" in the prosperous north.
His remarks, in a television interview on Wednesday night, suggested the centre-left government was now switching from a low-key approach of minimising and mocking Bossi's move.

The firebrand separatist, who has paved the way for Sunday's events with a flurry of headline-grabbing inflammatory statements, embarks on Friday on a three-day political pilgrimage from the source of the River Po.

The "March to the Sea" will climax on Sunday in Venice with Bossi's proclamation, accompanied by League rallies at 150 points along the 625-km (390-mile) river which the movement hopes will draw more than a million supporters.
A raft of counter-rallies is scheduled for the same day.
Prodi told RAI television he was "concerned but calm" while warning that the government would not tolerate any illegal act or breach of a constitutional commitment to national unity.

"This is a great country, and it must not meet the same end as Czechoslovakia, or even Yugoslavia," Prodi said. "Our example is Germany, which is even more united, not those countries which split, bringing grief to all their citizens."

Few, if any, political commentators believe Italians would take up arms for or against a northern breakaway, not least in the absence of the ethnic and religious rivalries that underpinned the bloodshed in former Yugoslavia.
But Prodi's centre-left government has faced political flak for not taking a tougher stand on Bossi's challenge.
"They're trying to brush me off as a clown and an adventurist clown...but as far as I'm concerned things have never been better," Bossi said last week.
The most prominent dissident from his League, former parliamentary Speaker Irene Pivetti, cautioned this week that to dismiss Bossi was a mistake.
"He is now serious about what he is doing. He really does want secession," she said in a magazine interview.

Bossi's movement built its support in the north, powerhouse of Italy's economy, over deep frustration with high taxes, bureaucracy and the scale of the political corruption that sank the country's old governing class.

While there is little sign that secession has a strong following in the north, where Bossi polled 3.7 million votes at the last general election in April, the slow pace of promised federal reform appears to be playing into the movement's hands.
An opinion poll in this week's Famiglia Cristiana magazine found that only one in 20 northern voters would follow Bossi wholeheartedly down the road to secession.
But it also said that the number of Italians who shared the view that unity was "an unsurrenderable benefit" had fallen to 53.9 percent from 58 percent in the last similar survey.
Bossi has been vague about what constitutes "Padania", defining it in social and economic terms -- a yardstick that pits the affluent north against Italy's less developed south.
His lieutenant Roberto Maroni said this week that on those terms the self-styled republic could stretch as far south as the central region of Umbria, knocking at the gates of Rome.

In the absence of ethnic or linguistic rallying calls, Bossi has also proved adept at creating a "Padanian" mythology for his followers that ranges from his mystification of the Po to unashamed plagiarism of non-Italian icons.

He has cited Gandhi as his model for non-violent action, compared himself to 13th century Scotsman William "Braveheart" Wallace for his independence battle and borrowed from the American declaration of independence for Sunday's proclamation.
